1177.title: Why God became man (ST III.1)
1177.hook: Thomas speaks of fittingness: nothing more fitting than God sharing our nature
1177.howItsDone: Catholics profess the incarnation in the Creed at Sunday Mass, bowing at the words about Christ becoming man, and kneeling at those words on Christmas and the Annunciation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grace: God's help, which heals our nature and lifts it. Your line was help is needed.

Her friend's father has died, across the country. A card would be kind. Flowers would be kind. Instead she books a flight, takes time off work, and is standing on the porch when the door opens. Nothing required it. But everyone in that house knows it was exactly the right thing, the thing that fit. Thomas Aquinas opens the third part of his Summa with that kind of question about God. Could God have helped us another way? And if so, why become one of us?
screen: `A CARD WOULD HAVE BEEN KIND.` → `SHE SHOWS UP AT THE DOOR.` → `WHY BECOME ONE OF US?`

segments.voice: Thomas's key word here is fitting. Not necessary. Fitting. He starts with what God is: goodness itself. And goodness, Thomas says, following an old Christian writer named Dionysius, is the kind of thing that pours itself out. So it belongs to the highest good to share itself in the highest way. What higher way than joining a created nature to himself, so that God and a human being are one person? That's the incarnation, God with skin, as day three hundred three put it. John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." Was it necessary? Couldn't God simply have forgiven, by a word? Thomas says yes, he could have. Nothing forced his hand. But some things are needed the way a horse is needed for a journey: not because the journey is impossible without it, but because it goes so much better. And this way does more. It gives faith firmer footing, because God himself is speaking. It gives hope. It stirs love, because nothing moves a person to love like being loved first. It gives an example to follow. And it opens the door to a surprising gift: sharing in God's own life. Thomas quotes Augustine's bold line: God became man so that man might become God. Second Peter says: "partakers of the divine nature." So Thomas's answer to why is not a mechanism. It's a kind of beauty. Of all the ways God might have helped, he sees none that fits better than coming in person and standing at the door.

Why God became man. Thomas's answer: not because God had to, but because, for the highest good, sharing itself in person was the most fitting way. Today's word.

1178.title: Sacraments as instruments (ST III.62)
1178.hook: God uses sacraments like a craftsman uses tools
1178.howItsDone: Catholics receive the sacraments as signs through which Christ gives grace, and the Church teaches that they work by the action of Christ himself, not by the holiness of the minister.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why God became man: not forced, but the fitting way for goodness to share itself. Your line was most fitting.

A violin lying in its case makes no music. Put it in a player's hands and the room is full. So who made the music? The player, obviously. And yet it's not the player's voice you're hearing. It's the violin's, with the grain of that wood in it. Back on day one hundred twenty-five, a sacrament was a sign that does something. Thomas asks who is really doing it, through water, oil, bread, words. His answer turns on a craftsman and a tool.
screen: `A VIOLIN IN ITS CASE IS SILENT.` → `IN A PLAYER'S HANDS, MUSIC.` → `WHO DOES THE WORK?`

segments.voice: Thomas sorts causes into two kinds. A principal cause works by its own power, the way fire heats. An instrumental cause works because something greater moves it. His picture is a carpenter and an axe. The bed looks like the plan in the carpenter's head, not like the axe. But the carpenter really works through it. So, Thomas says, God is the principal cause of grace, and the sacraments are his instruments. Baptism's water doesn't hold grace like a jar holds coins. God gives grace through it, the way the carpenter cuts through the axe. Then a detail that makes this more than a metaphor. An instrument has its own action too. The axe cuts because it's sharp; that's exactly how it serves the carpenter. In the same way, water washes. Bread feeds. Oil soothes. The sign isn't arbitrary: the sacrament's own action is the shape God's work takes. That's why Paul, in the Douay-Rheims, can speak of being saved "by the laver of regeneration, and renovation of the Holy Ghost." A laver is a washing basin. The washing is the instrument; the new life is God's. One more step. Thomas calls Christ's own humanity an instrument joined to God, like a hand. The sacraments are instruments set apart, like a tool that hand picks up. So grace flows from God, through Christ, through the sacrament, to a person. Christians understand sacraments in different ways; some churches see baptism and the Lord's Supper mainly as signs and acts of obedience. Thomas's picture is that God really works through the tool.

1179.title: Substance and appearance (ST III.75)
1179.hook: Thomas explains transubstantiation: the substance changes while appearances remain
1179.carry: what it is, not how it looks
1179.howItsDone: Catholics genuflect toward the tabernacle where the Eucharist is reserved, receive Communion at Mass, and some parishes hold Eucharistic adoration, where people sit or kneel in prayer before the host.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sacraments as instruments: God the craftsman, the sacrament his tool. Your line was God's tools.

At a family reunion, an old woman squints across the yard at a tall man with a gray beard and a cane. She doesn't recognize him. His hair is gone, he's far heavier than the skinny kid she used to babysit. Then he laughs, and she says his name. Everything about how he looks has changed. Who he is hasn't. Hold on to that, because Thomas Aquinas is about to turn it inside out. Today, the word he builds his account of the Eucharist on: substance.
screen: `EVERYTHING ABOUT HOW HE LOOKS CHANGED.` → `WHO HE IS DIDN'T.` → `NOW TURN IT INSIDE OUT.`

segments.voice: Thomas uses two words from philosophy. Substance is what a thing is. Accidents are the features it has: color, size, taste, weight, place. Usually the accidents change and the substance stays, like the man at the reunion. At Mass, Thomas says, it happens the other way around. At the Last Supper Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Take ye, and eat. This is my body." The Catholic Church takes those words literally. The whole substance of the bread is changed into the substance of Christ's body, and the wine into his blood, while the accidents remain: the color, taste and weight of bread and wine. The Church names this transubstantiation, first met on day one hundred fourteen: a change of substance. Thomas is careful about what it isn't. Christ's body doesn't travel down from heaven and push the bread aside. Nothing moves. It's a change in what is there, not where something goes. Why keep the look and taste of bread? People don't eat human flesh, and it would horrify them; so the gift comes as ordinary food. And it leaves room for faith. Are the senses fooled, then? No, he says. The senses judge appearances, and the appearances really are there. It's the mind, by faith, that knows what is underneath. In John, Jesus says: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Christians understand this differently. Orthodox Christians also speak of a real change, without Thomas's terms; some Protestant churches understand the bread as a sign or memorial. Thomas's word asks you to look past how something looks to what it is.

1180.title: The Corpus Christi hymns (1264)
1180.hook: the pope asks Thomas to write the texts for the new feast
1180.howItsDone: Catholics sing the Tantum ergo at Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament, and the Pange lingua accompanies the procession of the Eucharist at the end of the Holy Thursday Mass and on the feast of Corpus Christi.

segments.voice: Yesterday, substance: what a thing is, beneath how it looks, and Thomas's account of the change at Mass. Your line was what it is, not how it looks.
screen: `WHAT IT IS, NOT HOW IT LOOKS.`

segments.voice: Pages of careful argument: substance, accidents, a change that moves nothing. Then the same man is handed a different job. Tradition says Pope Urban the Fourth, setting up a new feast for the Body of Christ, asked Thomas Aquinas to write its texts: the prayers, the antiphons, the hymns to be sung. So the professor who wrote the Summa sits down to write songs. And the songs he's credited with are still sung at Benediction, at processions, on Holy Thursday night. Today: what happens when a theologian has to make it rhyme.
screen: `PAGES OF CAREFUL ARGUMENT.` → `A NEW FEAST NEEDS HYMNS.` → `THE PROFESSOR WRITES SONGS.`

segments.voice: Start with the first line of the Pange lingua: "Pange, lingua, gloriosi Corporis mysterium." Sing, my tongue, the mystery of the glorious body. Those first three words weren't new. An older hymn of the cross, by the poet Venantius Fortunatus, opens with the same three. Thomas takes the old opening and turns it from the cross to the altar: the cross and the Eucharist, in one echo. Then listen to what he does with yesterday's lesson. In the fourth verse: "Verbum caro, panem verum verbo carnem efficit." The Word made flesh, by his word, makes true bread into flesh. Word and flesh, flesh and word, chasing each other across one line: the incarnation and the Eucharist, folded into wordplay a choir can sing. The same verse goes on: even if the senses fail, faith alone is enough to steady a sincere heart. And the hymn's last two verses, sung on their own, became the Tantum ergo, the Benediction hymn from day one hundred forty-one: "Tantum ergo Sacramentum veneremur cernui." So great a sacrament, let us bow down and worship. A few lines later: "Praestet fides supplementum sensuum defectui." Let faith supply what the senses lack. It's yesterday's question about bread that still tastes like bread, answered not in an argument but in a song. The Summa works it out over pages; the hymn hands it to a choir. Same man, same truth, two ways of holding it.

If you pray, let it be your prayer; if you don't, simply notice what it's like to say an old line slowly.

1181.title: Adoro te devote
1181.hook: Hopkins translated it: Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore
1181.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Adoro te devote during Eucharistic adoration and before or after Communion, either in Latin or in English versions, including Hopkins's translation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Corpus Christi hymns: Pange lingua, and its last verses, the Tantum ergo. Your line was sing, my tongue.

A poet sits with a Latin hymn and tries to carry it over into English without spilling any. The poet is Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest whose own poems bend English into strange new music. The hymn is one tradition credits to Thomas Aquinas, a quiet prayer before the Eucharist. Its first words are Adoro te devote: I adore you devoutly. And Hopkins opens with a line that turns a doctrine into a picture: Godhead here in hiding, whom I do adore. Yesterday's hymns were for processions and choirs. This one is for one person, kneeling.
screen: `A POET AND A LATIN HYMN.` → `ADORO TE DEVOTE.` → `GODHEAD HERE IN HIDING.`

segments.voice: The Latin opening: "Adoro te devote, latens Deitas." I adore you devoutly, hidden Godhead. Latens means lying hidden. The whole hymn is built on that: God present, but out of sight. Scripture knew the idea. Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Verily thou art a hidden God, the God of Israel the saviour." Then the second verse goes straight at the senses: "Visus, tactus, gustus in te fallitur." Sight, touch and taste are deceived in you. Here's a wrinkle. Two days ago, in the Summa, Thomas was careful to say the senses are not deceived at Mass, because the appearances of bread really are there. The hymn speaks from the pew: the eyes see bread, the tongue tastes bread, and they can't reach what's underneath. Some readers put it this way: one is explaining; the other is kneeling. So what's left to trust? The hymn answers: hearing. "Sed auditu solo tuto creditur." Only by hearing is it safely believed. Hearing the word of Christ, who said this is my body. Paul, in Romans: "Faith then cometh by hearing; and hearing by the word of Christ." The hymn goes on, in effect: I believe whatever the Son of God has said, for nothing is truer than Truth's own word. That's the whole movement of the prayer: the eyes come up empty, the ears catch a word, and the heart bows. Scholars have debated whether Thomas wrote it himself; tradition keeps his name on it. Either way, it sounds like someone who spent his life thinking about what can't be seen.

1182.title: To contemplate and hand on (ST II-II.188.6)
1182.hook: better to light others than only to shine
1182.howItsDone: Dominicans describe their life with the phrase contemplata aliis tradere, to hand on what has been contemplated, and Catholics draw on Thomas's article when they speak about prayer feeding teaching and preaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Adoro te devote, the hymn tradition gives to Thomas, adoring a God hidden under bread. Your line was godhead here in hiding.

A friend finishes a book that changed something in them, and for a week your phone keeps buzzing. A photo of a page. A line underlined twice. "You have to read this." Whatever lit them up, they can't keep it to themselves. Thomas Aquinas asked a question that sounds dry and isn't: which is the better life, one spent quietly gazing at God, or one spent busy doing good? His answer was neither, exactly.
screen: `YOU HAVE TO READ THIS.` → `GAZING, OR DOING?` → `THOMAS SAYS: NEITHER, EXACTLY.`

segments.voice: The question sits near the end of the long second part of the Summa, where Thomas weighs different ways of religious life. Some communities mostly pray, in silence. Some mostly serve: nursing, feeding, building. Thomas says contemplation, looking at God in prayer, is the higher thing in itself. But he puts a third kind of life highest of all: contemplating, and then handing on to others what you've seen. Teaching. Preaching. His picture is a lamp. It's a greater thing to give light than only to shine. A lamp glowing in an empty room is lovely; a lamp that lets someone find the door does more. The Latin phrase that comes out of this article is contemplata aliis tradere, to hand on to others what you've contemplated. Tradition says Thomas's own order, the Dominicans, took it as a motto. Notice the order: first you look, then you give. Thomas isn't praising busy people who never stop to pray, or people who only talk. The handing on has to come out of real looking, or there's nothing to hand on. Elsewhere in the Summa he points to the life of Jesus himself, who taught out of his own prayer. In the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "So let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works." One honest note: this is Thomas's argument, and the Church holds all these callings dear. Enclosed nuns who pray for the world, and sisters who run a hospital, aren't failing a test. Thomas is describing the shape of a gift: what you receive in silence grows when it's given away.

1183.title: The crucifix in Naples
1183.hook: tradition says Christ asked what reward he wanted and Thomas answered only you, Lord
1183.howItsDone: Some Catholics retell this story on Thomas's feast day, and Thomas's answer, non nisi te, Domine, is sometimes painted or carved near images of him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, to contemplate and hand on: Thomas's lamp, giving light and not only shining. Your line was light others. Today closes the week.

"What do you want?" It's the question a cartoon genie asks, and the one a good friend asks when you go quiet at dinner. It sounds easy. It almost never is. The answer comes out as a list: a raise, a cure, a little more time, for a certain person to call back. There's a story in which someone asks Thomas Aquinas exactly that, and the one asking is Christ. His answer is very short.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT?` → `THE ANSWER COMES OUT AS A LIST.` → `CHRIST ASKS THOMAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the story as tradition tells it, from the people who gathered memories of Thomas after his death. It's set in Naples, in the Dominican house. Thomas is praying before a crucifix in the chapel. A brother nearby hears a voice from the cross. It says, in effect: Thomas, you have written well of me. What reward will you have for your work? And Thomas answers: non nisi te, Domine. Nothing but you, Lord. Be honest about what kind of story this is: a holy memory, handed down, not something you can check like a receipt. Catholics are free to weigh it as they like. But look at what it chooses to say. This is the man of the long Summa, with its objections and replies, its five ways and careful distinctions. And when the moment comes, he doesn't ask for his books to last, or his arguments to win, or even for understanding. He asks for a person. That fits what Thomas wrote. In the Summa he says our final happiness is seeing God, and that charity is friendship with God. Friends don't really want the gifts. They want the friend. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims sounds the same note: "For what have I in heaven? and besides thee what do I desire upon earth?" Look back at this week: God who fittingly shares our nature, sacraments as his tools, bread whose substance changes, hymns for Corpus Christi, a God here in hiding, a lamp that lights others. In this story, all of it comes down to one answer.

segments.voice: Let the question come plainly: what do you want? Let the list come too, the job, the health, the person, without pushing any of it away; then ask, underneath the list, what you want most, and it's all right if the answer surprises you, or doesn't come. If you pray, bring Thomas's short answer to God and see whether it fits.
